stem: President Jefferson had long argued for a strict reading of the Constitution, with only the powers it plainly gave. What does his purchase of Louisiana best show?

options.text: He followed strict construction exactly and refused every power not written down in the Constitution.
options.misconception: Buying Louisiana used a power the Constitution never mentions; a strict reading would have blocked it.

options.text: He believed the Constitution clearly gave presidents the power to buy land.
options.misconception: The Constitution says nothing about buying land; Jefferson himself worried the purchase was unconstitutional.

options.text: He set aside strict construction because the chance to buy Louisiana was too valuable to lose.
He asked the Supreme Court to write a new amendment before signing the treaty.
options.misconception: Jefferson thought about seeking an amendment, but he signed the treaty first and never got one.

rationales.A: Buying Louisiana used a power the Constitution never mentions. A strict reading would have blocked it.
rationales.B: The Constitution says nothing about buying land. Jefferson himself worried the purchase was unconstitutional.
rationales.C: Jefferson believed in strict construction, but the offer was too good to refuse. Background: he signed the treaty and asked Congress to pay, putting the nation's gain ahead of his own constitutional doubts.
rationales.D: Jefferson thought about seeking an amendment, but he signed the treaty first and never got one.
rationales.general:
1. Start with Jefferson's rule. The Constitution gives only the powers it plainly lists.
2. Check the purchase against that rule. Buying foreign land is nowhere in the list.
3. Ask what Jefferson did anyway. He signed, because Louisiana secured the Mississippi and doubled the nation.
4. Put it together. His principles bent when the prize was large enough.
Remember: even a strict reader of the Constitution can stretch it for a great prize.
